subject: Science
source: Based on the uploaded Class 6 Curiosity, Chapter 1 PDF (fecu101.pdf), Reprint 2026–27. Explanations and questions below are original supplementary material.
goals: Explain science as a systematic way to investigate questions about the natural and human-made world.
Distinguish an observation from an inference and a testable question.
Plan a fair investigation by changing one factor at a time where practical.
Record evidence carefully and use it to support a conclusion.
Recognise that scientific explanations can improve when new evidence appears.
summary: Science is not simply a collection of facts to memorise. It is a way of asking questions, observing carefully, testing ideas, recording evidence and revising explanations when evidence requires it. Curiosity begins an investigation; careful methods make its results more dependable.

concepts.title: Curiosity starts inquiry
concepts.explanation: A question such as ‘Why does a wet cloth dry faster in some places than others?’ can lead to an investigation. A useful question is specific enough that evidence could help answer it.
concepts.example: Instead of asking ‘What is weather like?’, ask ‘Does a wet cloth dry faster in moving air than in still air when both are kept in the same room?’

concepts.title: Observe before explaining
concepts.explanation: An observation is information collected using senses or instruments. An inference is an explanation drawn from observations. Keeping them separate helps prevent guesses from being mistaken for facts.
concepts.example: Observation: a metal spoon feels cooler than a wooden spoon in the same room. Inference: the metal may transfer heat away from the hand faster. The feeling alone does not prove the metal has a lower temperature.

concepts.title: Make a test fair
concepts.explanation: When testing one factor, keep other relevant conditions as similar as possible. Repeat measurements when possible and record results rather than selecting only the result you expected.
concepts.example: To compare drying, use two similar pieces of cloth with the same amount of water. Keep room temperature and cloth size similar, and vary only air movement.

concepts.title: Evidence supports conclusions
concepts.explanation: A conclusion should match the evidence collected. If results disagree with the original prediction, report the results honestly and consider possible reasons or a better test.
concepts.example: If the cloth in moving air dries first in repeated trials, the evidence supports the idea that moving air helped it dry faster under those conditions.

concepts.title: Science is collaborative and revisable
concepts.explanation: Scientists share methods and results so others can check them. Explanations may become more precise as better instruments, observations and experiments become available.
concepts.example: A first measurement may be rough. A more precise instrument can reveal differences that were too small to notice earlier.

workedExamples.question: A student wants to find out whether sunlight affects how quickly a puddle of water disappears. How can the student plan a fair comparison?
steps: Use two equal shallow containers with the same amount of water.
Place one in sunlight and the other in shade, keeping the containers in the same general environment.
Measure the remaining water at the same time intervals with the same method.
Repeat the comparison if possible and record all readings.
Compare the readings before making a conclusion; temperature and airflow may also affect evaporation and should be noted.
workedExamples.answer: Change the exposure to sunlight while measuring water loss consistently and acknowledging other conditions that could affect the result.

workedExamples.question: A plant near a window bends toward the light. State one observation and one possible inference.
steps: Describe only what can be directly seen: the stem curves toward the window.
Then suggest a possible explanation: the plant may be responding to the direction of light.
A further investigation would compare plants under different light directions.
workedExamples.answer: Observation: the stem curves toward the window. Inference: directional light may influence the plant’s growth.

practice.question: Write one testable question about how shadows change during a day.
practice.answer: Example: ‘Does the length of a fixed object’s shadow change between morning and noon?’
practice.why: It names a measurable feature and a comparison that can be observed.

practice.question: Why should results be recorded even when they do not match a prediction?
practice.answer: Because conclusions must be based on evidence, not on what the investigator hoped would happen.
practice.why: Ignoring unexpected results can create a misleading conclusion.

practice.question: A student says, ‘The floor is wet, so it must have rained.’ What is the problem with this statement?
practice.answer: The wet floor is an observation; rain is only one possible explanation. Someone may have spilled water or cleaned the floor.
practice.why: One observation can have several possible causes.

practice.question: Name two ways to improve the reliability of a simple measurement.
practice.answer: Repeat the measurement and use an appropriate, clearly marked measuring instrument; record units and method.
practice.why: Repeated readings and consistent methods help reveal errors.

mcqs.q: Which is the clearest example of an observation?
options: The plant’s leaves droop at midday
The plant needs exactly 2 hours of sun
mcqs.why: It describes something directly seen without assigning a cause.

mcqs.q: What should a fair test usually do?
options: Change one main factor and control others
Use only the result that supports the prediction
mcqs.why: Controlling other relevant conditions helps identify the effect of the factor being tested.

mcqs.q: A prediction in science is best described as…
options: A result that must be true
A statement that can be checked with evidence
mcqs.why: A scientific prediction can be compared with observations or test results.

options: To check consistency and reduce the effect of random error
mcqs.why: Repeated readings help assess whether a result is consistent.

mcqs.q: If evidence contradicts a prediction, the investigator should…
options: Report the evidence and reconsider the explanation
mcqs.why: Scientific explanations must respond to evidence, including unexpected results.

mcqs.q: Which sequence is most sensible for a basic investigation?
mcqs.why: A focused question guides a plan; evidence is collected before a conclusion is made.

revision: Science is a process of inquiry, not only a list of facts.
Observation describes evidence; inference proposes an explanation.
A fair test controls relevant conditions and changes the factor being investigated.
Record all results, repeat measurements where possible, and state limitations.
A conclusion must be supported by evidence and can be revised when new evidence appears.

chapterTest.instructions: Answer without opening the explanations. Then check the answer key and revise any concept you missed.

questions.q: Give one example of a question that can be investigated scientifically.
questions.answer: Any focused, testable question, such as whether a paper plane’s flight distance changes with wing shape.

questions.q: Explain the difference between an observation and an inference using an example.
questions.answer: Observation: the ground is wet. Inference: it may have rained; other causes are possible.

questions.q: Why is it important to keep conditions similar in a comparison?
questions.answer: It reduces the chance that another factor, rather than the factor being studied, caused the difference.

questions.q: What should you do if repeated trials produce different results?
questions.answer: Record each result, check the method and possible sources of variation, repeat carefully if possible, and avoid hiding the differences.

questions.q: A student tests two paper towels but uses different amounts of water on them. What makes the test unfair?
questions.answer: The starting amount of water differs, so water quantity is an uncontrolled factor. Use equal amounts and otherwise similar conditions.
